148.title: The god with the blue throat
148.hook: the ocean is churned, a poison rises, and Shiva drinks it; why Shivaratri is a night of pouring and keeping awake
148.carry: shiva drank the poison; we keep him company
148.tomorrow: The sign of the endless light
148.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a vigil through the four watches of the night, bathe the Shiva lingam with water, milk, yogurt, ghee or honey, offer bilva leaves, and chant Om Namah Shivaya until dawn; many remember Shiva as Nilakantha, who drank the poison from the churned ocean.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi's goodbye: the clay given back to the water, and come early next year. Your line was visarjan: god stays when the clay goes.
screen: `GANESH CHATURTHI: VISARJAN: GOD STAYS WHEN THE CLAY GOES.`

segments.voice: The gods and the asuras, their old rivals, agree on one thing for once. Together they'll churn the ocean of milk and pull out amrita, the nectar that makes you immortal. A mountain for a churning stick. A giant serpent for a rope. But the first thing to rise out of the ocean isn't nectar. It's halahala, a poison so strong its fumes start to burn the worlds. Gods and asuras drop the rope and run. They run to Shiva. And Shiva, without a speech, cups the poison in his hand and drinks it.
screen: `THE OCEAN IS CHURNED.` → `A POISON RISES.` → `SHIVA DRINKS IT.`

segments.voice: In many tellings, Parvati, his wife, catches him by the throat so the poison can't go down, and there it stays, turning his throat blue. That's why Shiva is called Nilakantha, the blue-throated one, and why so many pictures show him with a blue neck. Hindus remember Shiva for it as the god who takes in what would destroy everyone else. Many families connect this story to Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva you met on day eighty-three. It's one of several reasons people give for the night. The day starts with a fast. At sunset the vigil begins, split into four watches called praharas, each about three hours, each with its own worship. All night comes abhisheka: water and milk, sometimes yogurt, ghee and honey, poured slowly over the Shiva lingam, with bilva leaves, three to a stem, laid on top. Many devotees say the cool pouring soothes the god who held fire in his throat. And there's jagarana, keeping awake. One telling says people stayed up that night singing to Shiva while he held the poison, and devotees still keep him company, chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn. So the vigil isn't just endurance. It's love for the one who swallowed the world's poison. And today: when someone you love is carrying something hard so the rest of you don't have to, Shivaratri's answer is simple. Don't leave them alone with it. Sit up with them.
screen: `NILAKANTHA: THE BLUE THROAT.` · `A FAST, THEN FOUR WATCHES.` · `ABHISHEKA: THE COOL POURING.` · `JAGARANA: KEEPING AWAKE.` · then, large: `DON'T LEAVE THEM ALONE WITH IT.`

segments.voice: Here's a Shivaratri practice you can do at home. Take a little water and pour it slowly, over a lingam if you have one, or into a bowl or onto a plant. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya once with each pour. If you don't, just pour slowly and think of someone who's carrying something heavy right now. Breathe out as the water runs. Then sit for a minute and keep them company in your mind, the way a temple keeps Shiva company all night.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept awake with water and milk poured over the lingam, for the god with the blue throat.

149.title: The sign of the endless light
149.hook: a pillar of light with no end, a flower that lied, and why Shiva is worshipped as a smooth stone
149.carry: the lingam is a sign of the endless light
149.howItsDone: Many Hindus remember the Lingodbhava, Shiva appearing from an endless pillar of light, on Maha Shivaratri; they worship Shiva in the lingam, a sign of that light, temples often show the scene carved on the back wall of the shrine, and the twelve jyotirlinga temples draw crowds through the night.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poison from the churned ocean, the blue throat, and milk poured until dawn. Your line was shiva drank the poison; we keep him company.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: WE KEEP HIM COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing over who matters more when a column of fire bursts up between them, with no top and no bottom. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Neither finds an end, and Vishnu comes back and says so. You heard that on day ninety. Tonight, look again at two things. A small, sweet-smelling flower, drifting down out of the dark. And the pillar itself, which didn't stay in the story. You'll find it at the center of almost every Shiva temple.
screen: `A PILLAR WITH NO END.` → `A FLOWER DRIFTING DOWN.` → `IN EVERY SHIVA TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the flower has a name: ketaki, the fragrant screwpine blossom. Brahma, worn out and empty-handed, meets it falling from far above, and asks a favor. Back me up. The flower agrees. Brahma claims he reached the top, and the ketaki says yes, I saw him there. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out. Vishnu, who admitted his limit, is honored. Brahma is rebuked, and the flower gets its own sentence: never to be offered in Shiva's worship. Now the pillar. Walk into a Shiva temple and at the center you usually won't find a statue with a face. You'll find a smooth, rounded stone on a base: the lingam. Linga means sign, or mark. Hindus understand it as a sign of that pillar: Shiva as light with no top and no bottom, the God no single shape can hold. That's the teaching. The lingam isn't a portrait of Shiva. It points to what can't be pictured. Hindus also speak of twelve jyotirlingas, jyotis meaning light, shrines where Shiva is said to have shown himself as that light: Somnath on the Gujarat coast, Kashi Vishwanath in Varanasi, Kedarnath in the Himalayas, Rameshwaram in the far south, and eight more. This is a Shaiva story, told by Shiva's devotees; Vaishnava Hindus tell stories where Vishnu is the source, and Hindus hold these side by side. And today: when a friend asks why Hindus pray to a stone, you have the answer. It's not the stone. It's what the stone points to.
screen: `THE KETAKI SAYS YES.` · `THE FALSE WITNESS IS BARRED.` · `LINGA: A SIGN.` · `JYOTIRLINGA: TWELVE SHRINES OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `IT POINTS TO WHAT CAN'T BE PICTURED.`

segments.voice: Picture a smooth dark stone in front of you, with water running down it. Now let it stretch upward, past the ceiling, and downward, past the floor, with no end either way, just light. You can't see the top. You don't need to. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya once. Then let the picture settle back into a small stone, and notice that it still points to all of that.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, which many say remembers the pillar of light that had no end.

150.title: The thread and the king
150.hook: Lakshmi ties a thread on a king's wrist to bring Vishnu home; why the rakhi prayer names King Bali
150.carry: a rakhi binds a promise you keep
150.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravan, many Hindu sisters perform a small arti for their brothers, apply a tilak, tie a rakhi on the wrist while a short verse naming King Bali may be said, and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection, and today rakhis are also tied between sisters, cousins and friends.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pillar of light with no end, and a flower that lied. Your line was the lingam is a sign of the endless light.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: A SIGN OF THE ENDLESS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: There was once a king named Bali, an asura king, and he never said no to anyone who asked him for anything. That habit cost him his whole kingdom; on day one hundred fifty-four you'll hear how. He ended up ruling a world below this one, and Vishnu, moved by his goodness, promised to stand guard at his door. Which left Vishnu's wife, the goddess Lakshmi, alone at home. So one full moon, many families say, she goes down to Bali's palace in disguise, with a thread in her hand.
screen: `A KING WHO NEVER SAID NO.` → `VISHNU GUARDS HIS DOOR.` → `LAKSHMI, WITH A THREAD.`

segments.voice: She ties the thread on Bali's wrist and calls him brother. A sister! Ask for anything. And Lakshmi asks for the one thing she came for: the guard at your door. Bali, who has never broken his word, lets Vishnu go home. It's a story many families tell for Raksha Bandhan, and though it isn't in the oldest texts, it echoes in the prayer. When the thread is tied, many priests and some families say a short Sanskrit verse that begins yena baddho bali raja. Its sense: with the thread that bound mighty King Bali, I bind you; hold fast, don't slip. Bound how? The old story says Vamana had him tied with Varuna's ropes, but many teachers read the real bond as his word: Bali never broke it. That's the teaching under the rakhi. Raksha means protection, bandhan a bond, and the thread is a promise made before God. In Hindu teaching, keeping your word is part of dharma, the right way to live, and Bali is a model of it: he kept his promises even when they cost him everything. In many homes, the sister circles a small lamp before her brother's face, puts a red tilak on his forehead, ties the thread on his right wrist, and feeds him a sweet. He gives a gift and a promise to protect her. Today rakhis are tied between sisters, cousins and close friends too. And today: a rakhi isn't a bracelet. It's a promise you can see on your wrist all week, and it asks Bali's question: will you keep it when it costs you something?
screen: `LAKSHMI TIES, BALI KEEPS HIS WORD.` · `YENA BADDHO BALI RAJA.` · `RAKSHA, PROTECTION. BANDHAN, A BOND.` · `LAMP, TILAK, THREAD, SWEET, PROMISE.` · then, large: `A PROMISE YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise you've made to someone, out loud or not: to show up, to look out for them, to call. If you have a thread, tie it on your wrist; if not, just rest your fingers where a rakhi would go. If you pray, say the name you pray to. Then make the promise again, silently, once, and hold your wrist for a few breaths. Then let your hand go.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection: a thread tied on the full moon of Shravan, with a promise that holds.

151.title: Bhishma waits for the sun
151.hook: a warrior on a bed of arrows waits for the sun to turn north; why families save good beginnings for after Sankranti
151.carry: uttarayana: the sun's bright half, when good things begin
151.howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, many Hindus bathe in rivers, give to those in need, share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Gujarat and elsewhere spend the day flying kites from rooftops to mark the sun's turn north into uttarayana, the auspicious half of the year when many families plan weddings and new beginnings.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan, and the king named in the thread's prayer. Your line was a rakhi binds a promise you keep.
screen: `RAKSHA BANDHAN: A PROMISE YOU KEEP.`

segments.voice: The great war of the Mahabharata, and the oldest warrior on the field goes down. Bhishma, great-uncle to both sides, is struck by so many arrows that when he falls, he never touches the ground. He lies on them like a bed. And Bhishma has a gift, a boon from long ago: he can choose the moment he dies. The pain is enormous. The war goes on around him. Everyone expects him to let go. He doesn't. He looks up at the sky and says he'll wait. For the sun.
screen: `THE OLDEST WARRIOR FALLS.` → `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE SUN.`

segments.voice: For weeks Bhishma lies there, and he doesn't waste the time. The family comes to him, and he teaches them about duty, kingship and God. Then the sun turns north, and only then does he let go. Why wait? Because the sun's northward half of the year, uttarayana, is held to be the bright, auspicious half: the best time to begin things, and a blessed time to leave the world. The day many Hindus mark that turn is Makar Sankranti. Sankranti means crossing: the sun crossing into Makara, the sign called Capricorn. Most festivals follow the moon, so their dates wander. This one follows the sun, so it lands in mid-January almost every year. Here's the teaching. For Hindus, time isn't all the same. Some times are shubh, auspicious, good for beginning, and families look up a muhurat, an auspicious moment, for a wedding, a new house, a first day. In many North Indian families, weddings pause in the month before Sankranti and start again once the sun has turned. And in Gujarat, whole cities climb onto their rooftops that day and fill the sky with kites. The old texts don't mention kites; the rooftops do. Some say they're thanks sent up toward the sun. And today: when your family waits for a good date, it isn't just superstition. It's the idea Bhishma held on for. What you begin, begin in the light.
screen: `BHISHMA WAITS FOR THE TURN.` · `UTTARAYANA: THE BRIGHT HALF.` · `SANKRANTI: THE SUN CROSSES.` · `SHUBH MUHURAT: A GOOD MOMENT.` · then, large: `BEGIN IN THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit where there's daylight if you can, or picture winter sun on your face. Think of one thing you'd like to begin: a habit, a conversation, a piece of work. Don't start it yet. Just hold it, the way Bhishma held on, and choose a moment to begin it, a morning, a day, on purpose. If you pray, offer it to the sun with folded hands, the way many Hindus greet Surya at dawn. Then breathe out slowly.
Makar Sankranti. The day the sun crosses into Makara and turns north, the start of the bright half of the year.

152.title: The sun visits his son
152.hook: the sun visits the son he grew apart from and is welcomed with black sesame; why Sankranti sweets come with sweet words

152.howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti many Hindus bathe at dawn in a river, give food, grain or blankets to those in need, and share sweets of sesame and jaggery with the words 'take this, and speak sweetly'; the day is kept as Lohri, Bhogali Bihu and Pongal in different regions.

segments.voice: Surya, the sun, has a son named Shani, the slow, serious planet people worry about. Their story isn't a happy one. In many tellings, Surya kept his distance from the boy, Shani grew up hurt, and father and son hardly spoke. But the sun keeps moving, sign to sign, all year. And Makara, the sign the sun enters at Sankranti, belongs in Hindu astrology to Shani. It's his house. So once a year the father arrives at his son's door. And the son has to decide how to open it.
screen: `A FATHER AND A SON, APART.` → `MAKARA IS SHANI'S HOUSE.` → `THE SUN AT HIS SON'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: As many families tell it, Shani's house had almost nothing in it. All he could offer was black sesame. He gave it to his father anyway, and Surya was moved, and blessed him, and father and son made peace. It's a folk story, not from the old epics, but it's one of the reasons people give for why sesame is everywhere on this day. In Maharashtra, people go visiting with little sweets of sesame and jaggery, the dark unrefined sugar, called til-gul. You hand one to a neighbor, a cousin, a friend you've had words with, and say: til-gul ghya, god god bola. Take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. Sesame is small and sticks together; jaggery is sweet. Here's the teaching. Hindus treat speech as part of dharma, the right way to live. An old Sanskrit verse puts it plainly: speak what is true, and speak it kindly. And Sankranti, the first day of the bright half, is a day for mending bonds and for dana, a gift given freely. People bathe at dawn, in a river if they can, and give sesame, grain, blankets or food to someone in need. In Punjab, the night before is Lohri, with bonfires; in Assam, Bhogali Bihu, a feast. And today: a sesame sweet is a small way to say what's hard to say out loud. Sorry. Let's start again. If a father and a son who barely spoke could do it at a door, two friends can do it with a sweet.

Maybe their face softens, maybe it doesn't; that part isn't yours. If you pray, ask for kind speech this year, in your own words. Your part is the sweet and the words.

153.title: The bull sent to plow
153.hook: Shiva's bull garbles a message and is sent to plow; why Pongal thanks the sun and the cattle, and why Hindus honor the cow
153.carry: thank the ones who feed you: sun and cow
153.howItsDone: Over four days in the Tamil month of Thai, many Tamil Hindus clear out old things on Bhogi, boil new rice with milk and jaggery until it overflows and offer it to the sun on Thai Pongal, bathe, garland and feed their cattle on Mattu Pongal, and visit family on Kaanum Pongal.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun at his son's door, and black sesame. Your line was sankranti mends bonds: sweet sesame, sweet words. Today, Tamil Nadu, and a pot meant to overflow.
screen: `MAKAR SANKRANTI: SWEET SESAME, SWEET WORDS.`

segments.voice: Up on Mount Kailash, Shiva gives his bull a simple errand. Nandi, called Basava in this story, is to go down to earth with a message for the people: bathe every day, and eat once a month. Nandi trots down, clears his throat, and announces: Shiva says, bathe once a month, and eat every day! Shiva is not amused. If people are going to eat every day, he says, somebody has to grow all that food. You'll go and plow the fields. And Nandi has been helping the farmers ever since.
screen: `A MESSAGE FROM SHIVA.` → `NANDI GETS IT BACKWARD.` → `SENT TO PLOW.`

segments.voice: That's a folk tale told in Tamil Nadu at Pongal, and it's a funny way of saying something serious. Pongal is Tamil Nadu's harvest festival, on the same days as Sankranti, at the start of the Tamil month of Thai. Pongal means boiling over. A new clay pot of fresh rice, milk and jaggery is set on a fire in the open sun, and when it foams over the side, everyone shouts Pongalo Pongal! The overflow is abundance you can see. And the first pongal goes to Surya, the sun, before anyone eats. The next day is the one the story is about: Mattu Pongal, for the cattle. Cows and bulls are bathed, their horns painted, bells and garlands put on them, and they're fed pongal too. Here's the teaching. Hindus honor the cow. Many call her Go Mata, mother cow, because like a mother she gives: milk, butter, ghee for the lamp, and for centuries a strong back to pull the plow. Krishna grew up herding cows, and Shiva rides a bull. That's a big reason many Hindus don't eat beef, and why you'll see a cow garlanded at a temple. Pongal turns that into days of thanks: first the sun that grew the rice, then the animals that did the work. A Tamil saying for the week: when Thai is born, a way will be born. And today: there's a long line of givers behind every plate you eat from. Pongal says thank them, starting with the ones nobody thanks.
screen: `PONGAL MEANS BOILING OVER.` · `THE FIRST SHARE TO THE SUN.` · `MATTU PONGAL: A DAY FOR THE CATTLE.` · `GO MATA: THE COW WHO GIVES.` · then, large: `THANK THE ONES WHO FEED YOU.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, or right now in your mind, follow your food backward: the hands that cooked it, the shop, the truck, the farmer, the rain and the sun, and any animal that gave. If you pray, offer the first bite in your heart, the way the first pongal goes to the sun. If you don't, just say thank you, once, to the giver you'd usually forget.

154.title: The king who gave himself
154.hook: a boy asks a king for three steps of land, and the king gives his own head; why Kerala welcomes Mahabali home at Onam
154.carry: bali gave himself: the highest offering
154.howItsDone: During the ten days of Onam in the Malayalam month of Chingam, many Hindus in Kerala lay a pookalam of flowers at the door that grows each day, wear new clothes, and share the Onam sadhya on banana leaves to welcome King Mahabali, remembered for giving himself to Vishnu as Vamana, on his yearly visit.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pongal: a pot boiling over for the sun, and a day for the cattle. Your line was thank the ones who feed you: sun and cow. Today, Kerala, and the king from the rakhi prayer.
screen: `PONGAL: THANK THE ONES WHO FEED YOU.`

segments.voice: In Kerala, in late summer, on the first morning of Onam, someone gets up early and lays a small circle of flower petals at the front door. Next morning, it grows a ring. And the next. For ten days it grows, a carpet of flowers called a pookalam, until by the last day it's a bright mandala across the doorstep. A guest is coming. A king, who wants to see that his people are happy. The same King Bali whose name is in the rakhi prayer.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF PETALS AT THE DOOR.` → `BIGGER EVERY MORNING FOR TEN DAYS.` → `A KING IS COMING.`

segments.voice: Mahabali was an asura, from the side usually cast as the gods' rivals. But in Kerala he's remembered as the best king there ever was. A Malayalam folk song still sung at Onam remembers his reign as a time when all people were equal: no lies, no cheating, no one poor. The gods grew worried about his power. So Vishnu came to him as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for just as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali's own teacher warned him: this boy is Vishnu, don't promise. Bali, who never refused anyone, said yes anyway. And the boy grew. One step covered the earth. The second, the heavens. There was nowhere left for the third, so Bali bowed and offered his own head. The Bhagavata Purana tells it as a story of devotion: Bali is honored, not destroyed, and Vishnu promises to guard his door. Here's the teaching. Bhakti, loving devotion to God, has many forms in the Hindu tradition. The tradition lists nine, and the last is atma-nivedana, offering yourself. Bali is its classic example. He gave more than land; he gave himself. Kerala adds one more thing: Bali asked to visit his people once a year, and Onam is that visit. So there's the pookalam, new clothes, and the sadhya, a vegetarian feast on a banana leaf. Keralites of many faiths join in. And today: Onam asks what you'd hold back from what you love most, and remembers the king who held back nothing.
screen: `AN ASURA, THE BEST OF KINGS.` · `THREE STEPS: EARTH, HEAVEN, HIS HEAD.` · `ATMA-NIVEDANA: OFFERING YOURSELF.` · `ONE VISIT A YEAR: ONAM.` · then, large: `HE HELD BACK NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Imagine Mahabali is visiting you this year, not to judge, just to see how you are. For each good thing in your life right now, lay one ring of petals at your door, and let the circle grow without rushing it. Then, if you pray, offer yourself the way Bali did, in your own words: here I am, all of me. If you don't pray, just sit beside the circle like someone waiting for a guest they love.
